title: Eggshell as Fertilizer: What It Does and How to Use It
metaTitle: Eggshell as Fertilizer: Does It Really Work?
metaDescription: Eggshell as fertilizer adds calcium, not nitrogen. Learn what crushed eggshells do for soil and plants, how to prepare them, and what they cannot fix.
excerpt: Using eggshell as fertilizer works, but only for one thing: calcium. Eggshells are almost pure calcium carbonate, the same material as garden lime. Crushed fine and mixed into the soil, they release calcium slowly and can raise the pH of acid soil a little. They add almost no nitrogen, phosphorus or potassium, so they cannot replace compost or a real fertilizer.

blocks.text:
Every kitchen throws away eggshells, so it is natural to ask whether they can feed the garden. The honest answer is yes, a little, in a slow and narrow way.

This guide explains what eggshells contain, how to prepare them, which plants gain, and the problems eggshells will not solve. For stronger organic choices, see our list of [organic fertilizer examples](/blog/organic-fertilizer-examples).
What is in eggshell as fertilizer

An eggshell is mostly calcium carbonate, about nine tenths or more of its weight. The rest is a thin protein membrane and very small amounts of magnesium, phosphorus and other minerals. So, as a fertilizer, an eggshell is really a slow form of lime.

Calcium matters to plants. It builds strong cell walls, helps roots grow, and keeps fruit firm. But most soils already hold some calcium, and acid soils are the ones most likely to lack it.

blocks.text: How to prepare eggshells for plants

items.title: Rinse them
items.text: Wash out the egg white so the shells do not smell or draw ants and rats.

items.title: Dry them
items.text: Sun dry them for a day or two. Some people also bake them briefly, which makes them easier to crush.

items.title: Grind them fine
items.text: This is the step that matters most. Big pieces sit in the soil for years. A fine powder, made in a mortar or an old blender, releases calcium much faster.

items.title: Mix into the soil or compost
items.text: Work the powder into the planting hole or bed, or add the shells to your compost pile, where they break down along with everything else.

blocks.title: Eggshell water gives very little
blocks.text: Soaking shells in water and pouring it on plants is popular online, but calcium carbonate barely dissolves in plain water. The plant gets very little from it. Powder in the soil does more.
Which plants gain from eggshell as fertilizer

items: **Tomato, pepper and eggplant:** fruiting crops that need steady calcium.
**Cabbage, pechay and other leafy greens:** they use calcium for firm, healthy leaves.
**Plants in acid soil:** where calcium is short and a little lime helps.
**Potted plants:** a pinch of powder in the potting mix at planting.

blocks.text: Skip eggshells on soils that are already alkaline, or for plants that like acid soil, because adding lime there pushes the pH the wrong way. If you are not sure of your soil, a soil test from your Municipal Agriculture Office tells you. Our guide on [acidic soil preparation](/land-preparation/acidic-soil-preparation) explains liming on a field scale.
Eggshells and blossom end rot in tomatoes

Blossom end rot is the dark, sunken spot at the bottom of a tomato fruit. It comes from too little calcium reaching the fruit. So many gardeners reach for eggshells.

But the cause is usually water, not a lack of calcium in the soil. When watering swings between dry and soaked, the plant cannot move calcium into the fruit fast enough, even in soil that has plenty. Shells added after the problem appears also break down too slowly to help that season. Even watering and mulch fix blossom end rot faster. Our guide on [fertilizer for tomatoes](/blog/fertilizer-for-tomatoes) covers the full feeding plan.

items: **They do not feed leaves.** A pale, yellow plant needs nitrogen, which eggshells do not have.
**They do not replace fertilizer.** For real growth you still need compost, manure or a fertilizer with N, P and K.
**They are a weak pest barrier.** Crushed shells around plants slow some snails and slugs a little, but do not count on them.
**They work slowly.** Think of them as a soil builder over many months, not a quick fix.

blocks.text: For richer organic feeding, compare [chicken dung as fertilizer](/blog/chicken-dung-as-fertilizer) and see our list of [organic fertilizer benefits](/blog/organic-fertilizer-benefits).

items.a: It is a slow source of calcium, not a complete fertilizer. It adds almost no nitrogen, phosphorus or potassium.

items.q: How do I use eggshells as fertilizer?
items.a: Rinse and dry them, grind them into a fine powder, and mix the powder into the soil or the planting hole, or add them to compost.

items.q: Do eggshells stop blossom end rot?
items.a: Not quickly. Blossom end rot usually comes from uneven watering, and shells break down too slowly to fix it in the same season.
Tomato, pepper, eggplant and leafy greens, especially in acid soil. Avoid them in alkaline soil or for plants that like acid soil.

items.q: How long do eggshells take to break down?
items.a: Coarse pieces can last years. A fine powder releases calcium over months, faster in acid soil.
